label is already used on the C bag).\n   117\t\n   118\tSo the Mixed content **can go on any of the three remaining labels**, because none of them say “Mixed”, so it won’t be a correct label (which is good, since original labeling had Mixed label on C bag, and Mixed bag is mislabeled, so it must not be labeled “Mixed” — which it isn’t).\n   119\t\n   120\tSo far so good.\n   121\t\n   122\tBut to **distinguish** which of the three remaining bags is Mixed vs pure M vs pure G, we likely need **more than one draw**.\n   123\t\n   124\tBecause if we pick from, say, the bag labeled “Chocolates”, and pull out a mint, it could be:\n   125\t- Pure M, or\n   126\t- Mixed bag that contains M (i.e., M+G or C+M)\n   127\t\n   128\tBut we already know C is taken, but Mixed could still be C+M.\n   129\t\n   130\tWait — but if Mixed were C+M, then chocolates would appear in two bags: pure C and Mixed. That’s allowed.\n   131\t\n   132\tSo pulling a mint from bag labeled “Chocolates” doesn’t tell us if it’s pure M or Mixed (C+M or M+G).\n   133\t\n   134\tSo ambiguity remains.\n   135\t\n   136\tHence, **one draw is not enough**.\n   137\t\n   138\t---\n   139\t\n   140\t### Step 4: Can we do it in **two** draws?\n   141\t\n   142\tIdea: First draw from bag labeled “Mixed” → identifies a pure type (say C).\n   143\t\n   144\tSecond draw: choose wisely to resolve the rest.\n   145\t\n   146\tWhich bag to draw from next?\n   147\t\n   148\tConsider drawing from **one of the pure-labeled bags**, say the one labeled “Chocolates”.\n   149\t\n   150\tBut maybe better: draw from a bag that, based on possible assignments, can disambiguate.\n   151\t\n   152\tAlternative idea: **Draw from the bag labeled “Chocolates”**.\n   153\t\n   154\tBut let’s think more systematically.\n   155\t\n   156\tAfter first draw (from “Mixed” → C), we know:\n   157\t\n   158\t- True C = bag labeled “Mixed”\n   159\t- Remaining true types: M, G, Mixed (pair unknown)\n   160\t\n   161\tNow, consider the bag labeled “Mints”. It cannot be M, so it’s either G or Mixed.\n   162\t\n   163\tSimilarly, bag labeled “Gum” ≠ G → so it’s M or Mixed.\n   164\t\n   165\tBag labeled “Chocolates” ≠ C → so it’s M, G, or Mixed.\n   166\t\n   167\tWe need to figure out which is which.\n   168\t\n   169\tSuppose we draw **one item from the bag labeled “Chocolates”**.\n   170\t\n   171\tPossible outcomes:\n   172\t\n   173\t- Get **M**: then this bag is either pure M or Mixed (C+M or M+G)\n   174\t- Get **G**: then either pure G or Mixed (C+G or M+G)\n   175\t- Get **C**: impossible! Because bag labeled “Chocolates” is not C (mislabeled), and only pure C bag is the one labeled “Mixed”. But wait — Mixed bag might contain C, so if this bag were Mixed and contained C, you could draw C.\n   176\t\n   177\tAh! Important: **bag labeled “Chocolates” could be the Mixed bag**, and if Mixed = C+M or C+G, then it contains C → so you **could** draw C from it.\n   178\t\n   179\tBut that would be confusing, because then you might think it’s pure C, but it’s not — but you already know pure C is the one labeled “Mixed”, and all bags are mislabeled, so bag labeled “Chocolates” cannot be pure C, but could be Mixed with C.\n   180\t\n   181\tSo if you draw C from bag labeled “Chocolates”, you know it must be **Mixed**, and specifically a mix that includes C (so C+M or C+G).\n   182\t\n   183\tThat’s useful!\n   184\t\n   185\tSimilarly, if you draw M from bag labeled “Mints”, that’s impossible if it’s pure M (not allowed), but could happen if it’s Mixed with M.\n   186\t\n   187\tSo perhaps **two draws** suffice.\n   188\t\n   189\tLet’s test worst-case scenario.\n   190\t\n   191\t#### Worst case: First draw from “Mixed” → C.\n   192\t\n   193\tNow, to identify the Mixed bag, we can use the fact that **only the Mixed bag can yield two different types**.\n   194\t\n   195\tBut we are only allowed to **inspect one item at a time**, and want to **minimize total inspections**.\n   196\t\n   197\tWe don’t have to fully empty a bag — just inspect enough to guarantee correct labeling.\n   198\t\n   199\tKey insight: **The Mixed bag is the only one that can possibly contain two types**, but we only see one item at a time.\n   200\t\n   201\tHowever, **pure bags will only ever give one type**.\n   202\t\n   203\tBut with **a single draw**, you can’t confirm if a bag is pure or mixed — unless you combine with logic from labeling constraints.\n   204\t\n   205\tLet’s consider this approach:\n   206\t\n   207\t1. Draw 1: from bag labeled “Mixed” → reveals pure type (say C). Now we know true C.\n   208\t\n   209\t2. Now, consider the two bags labeled with the **other two pure types** — i.e., “Mints” and “Gum”.\n   210\t\n   211\t   - Bag labeled “Mints” ≠ M → so it’s either G or Mixed.\n   212\t   - Bag labeled “Gum” ≠ G → so it’s either M or Mixed.\n   213\t\n   214\tNote that **only one** of these can be Mixed.\n   215\t\n   216\tSo if we draw from **one** of them, and get a candy that matches its **label**, that’s impossible — but we won’t.\n   217\t\n   218\tBut suppose we draw from bag labeled “Mints”:\n   219\t\n   220\t- If we get **G**, then this bag is either pure G or Mixed (M+G). But it can’t be pure G? Wait, yes it can — because its label is “Mints”, so pure G is allowed (just not M).\n   221\t\n   222\t- If we get **C**, then this bag must be Mixed (since pure G or M wouldn’t have C), and Mixed must be C+G or C+M.\n   223\t\n   224\tBut we already know C exists in pure bag, but that’s fine.\n   225\t\n   226\tNow, here’s a better idea inspired by classic solution:\n   227\t\n   228\t> **Draw one item from the bag labeled “Mixed” → identifies a pure type.**\n   229\t>\n   230\t> **Then draw one item from the bag labeled with that same type.**\n   231\t\n   232\tWait — the bag labeled with that type is mislabeled, so it’s not pure.\n   233\t\n   234\tExample: First draw from “Mixed” → C.\n   235\t\n   236\tNow, look at bag labeled “Chocolates”. It is mislabeled, so it's **not** pure C. So it must be M, G, or Mixed.\n   237\t\n   238\tNow, draw one item from bag labeled “Chocolates”.\n   239\t\n   240\tCase analysis:\n   241\t\n   242\t- If you draw **M**:\n   243\t  - Possibilities: pure M, or Mixed (C+M or M+G)\n   244\t  - But can it be pure M? Yes, because label is “Chocolates” ≠ M → allowed.\n   245\t  - Can it be Mixed? Yes.\n   246\t\n   247\t- If you draw **G**: similar.\n   248\t\n   249\t- If you draw **C**:\n   250\t  - Then it **must be Mixed**, because pure C is already identified, and this bag can't be pure C.\n   251\t  - So Mixed includes C.\n   252\t\n   253\tSo if second draw yields **C**, we immediately identify Mixed bag.\n   254\t\n   255\tThen the remaining two bags must be pure M and pure G, and we can assign them using the mislabeling constraint.\n   256\t\n   257\tFor example:\n   258\t- If bag labeled “Chocolates” is Mixed (contains C),\n   259\t- Then bags labeled “Mints” and “Gum” must be pure G and pure M, but not matching their labels.\n   260\t- So bag labeled “Mints” ≠ M → must be G\n   261\t- Bag labeled “Gum” ≠ G → must be M\n   262\t\n   263\tDone! Labels fixed.\n   264\t\n   265\tNow, what if second draw is **not C**, say it’s **M**?\n   266\t\n   267\tThen bag labeled “Chocolates” is either pure M or Mixed (M+G or C+M).\n   268\t\n   269\tBut we don’t know which.\n   270\t\n   271\tHowever, note: if it were **pure M**, then the Mixed bag must be either C+G or M+G.\n   272\t\n   273\tBut C+G doesn’t contain M; M+G does.\n   274\t\n   275\tNow, consider the bag labeled “Mints”. It cannot be M, so options: G or Mixed.\n   276\t\n   277\tSimilarly, bag labeled “Gum”: M or Mixed.\n   278\t\n   279\tWe still have ambiguity.\n   280\t\n   281\tBut here’s the catch: **Can we guarantee resolution in two draws in all cases?**\n   282\t\n   283\tConsider worst case: second draw gives **M** (not C). Now we don’t know if bag labeled “Chocolates” is pure M or Mixed.\n   284\t\n   285\tIf it’s pure M, then Mixed is either C+G or M+G.\n   286\t\n   287\tBut if Mixed = M+G, then both M and G appear in Mixed.\n   288\t\n   289\tBut we haven’t seen G yet.\n   290\t\n   291\tIs there a scenario where **two draws are insufficient**?\n   292\t\n   293\tYes. Suppose:\n   294\t\n   295\t- Draw 1 (from “Mixed”) → C → so true C = bag labeled “Mixed”\n   296\t- Draw 2 (from “Chocolates”) → M\n   297\t\n   298\tNow possibilities:\n   299\t\n   300\t**Possibility 1**: “Chocolates” bag = pure M  \n   301\t→ Then Mixed bag is either C+G or M+G  \n   302\tBut C+G doesn’t contain M, M+G does.\n   303\t\n   304\t**Possibility 2**: “Chocolates” bag = Mixed = C+M  \n   305\t→ Then pure M must be in either “Mints” or “Gum” bag.\n   306\t\n   307\tBut bag labeled “Mints” can’t be M, so pure M would have to be in bag labeled “Gum”.\n   308\t\n   309\tSimilarly, pure G would be in bag labeled “Mints”.\n   310\t\n   311\tNow, check consistency:\n   312\t\n   313\t- In Possibility 1 (Chocolates = pure M):\n   314\t  - Pure M = “Chocolates”\n   315\t  - Pure C = “Mixed”\n   316\t  - Remaining bags: “Mints” and “Gum” → must be G and Mixed\n   317\t  - “Mints” ≠ M → OK to be G or Mixed\n   318\t  - “Gum” ≠ G → OK to be M (but M already used) or Mixed → so “Gum” must be Mixed\n   319\t  - Then “Mints” = G\n   320\t\n   321\t  So Mixed = “Gum”\n   322\t\n   323\t- In Possibility 2 (Chocolates = Mixed = C+M):\n   324\t  - Pure C = “Mixed”\n   325\t  - Mixed = “Chocolates”\n   326\t  - Remaining: “Mints” and “Gum” → must be pure M and pure G\n   327\t  - “Mints” ≠ M → so must be G\n   328\t  - “Gum” ≠ G → so must be M\n   329\t\n   330\tBoth scenarios are logically consistent with all constraints and the two observations.\n   331\t\n   332\tAnd they lead to **different labelings**:\n   333\t\n   334\t- In P1: “Gum” is Mixed\n   335\t- In P2: “Chocolates” is Mixed\n   336\t\n   337\tSo with only two draws (C from “Mixed”, M from “Chocolates”), we **cannot distinguish** between these two cases.\n   338\t\n   339\tTherefore, **two draws are not sufficient in worst case**.\n   340\t\n   341\t---\n   342\t\n   343\t### Step 5: Try **three** draws\n   344\t\n   345\tCan we guarantee with **three**?\n   346\t\n   347\tStrategy:\n   348\t\n   349\t1. Draw from bag labeled “Mixed” → reveals pure type (say C).\n   350\t2. Draw from bag labeled “Chocolates” → suppose we get M.\n   351\t3. Now, draw from **one of the remaining bags**, say “Mints”.\n   352\t\n   353\tNow, third draw:\n   354\t\n   355\t- If from “Mints” we get **G**:\n   356\t  - “Mints” bag ≠ M → so could be pure G or Mixed.\n   357\t  - If it’s pure G, fine.\n   358\t  - If it’s Mixed, then Mixed contains G (so C+G or M+G)\n   359\t\n   360\tBut now combine all info.\n   361\t\n   362\tAlternatively, smarter: after first two draws, if second draw is **not C**, then **draw from the bag whose label matches the item you just drew**.\n   363\t\n   364\tIn example: second draw from “Chocolates” gave M → now draw from bag labeled “Mints”.\n   365\t\n   366\tWhy? Because bag labeled “Mints” cannot be pure M, so if you draw M from it, it must be Mixed.\n   367\t\n   368\tSimilarly, if you draw G, it could be pure G or Mixed.\n   369\t\n   370\tLet’s simulate worst-case distinguishing.\n   371\t\n   372\tFrom earlier, the ambiguous cases were:\n   373\t\n   374\t- Case A: “Chocolates” = pure M, “Gum” = Mixed\n   375\t- Case B: “Chocolates” = Mixed, “Gum” = pure M\n   376\t\n   377\tTo distinguish, check content of “Gum” bag.\n   378\t\n   379\tIn Case A: “Gum” = Mixed → contains either C+G or M+G\n   380\tIn Case B: “Gum” = pure M → only M\n   381\t\n   382\tSo draw one item from “Gum”:\n   383\t\n   384\t- If you get **M** → could be pure M or Mixed (if M+G)\n   385\t- If you get **G** → then “Gum” is either pure G (not allowed, label = Gum) → so must be Mixed\n   386\t- If you get **C** → then “Gum” = Mixed (C+G)\n   387\t\n   388\tBut if you get **M**, still ambiguous.\n   389\t\n   390\tBut note: in Case A, “Chocolates” = pure M, so all M items are in “Chocolates” (20) + possibly Mixed (“Gum”) if M+G.\n   391\t\n   392\tIn Case B, “Gum” = pure M (20), and “Chocolates” = Mixed (C+M) → also has 10 M.\n   393\t\n   394\tSo both can yield M.\n   395\t\n   396\tBut here’s key: **In Case A, the Mixed bag is “Gum”**, which must be either C+G or M+G.\n   397\t\n   398\tBut recall: we have **not seen G yet**.\n   399\t\n   400\tIf Mixed = C+G, then G appears only in “Gum”.\n   401\t\n   402\tIf Mixed = M+G, G appears in “Gum”.\n   403\t\n   404\tWhereas in Case B, Mixed = “Chocolates” = C+M → **no G in Mixed**, so G appears only in pure G bag, which would be “Mints”.\n   405\t\n   406\tSo to distinguish, maybe draw from “Mints”.\n   407\t\n   408\tThis is getting complex.\n   409\t\n   410\tBut perhaps there's a known result.\n   411\t\n   412\t### Known result analogy:\n   413\t\n   414\tIn the classic problem with 3 bags (A, O, Mixed), all mislabeled, **1 draw** suffices.\n   415\t\n   416\tHere, with 4 bags and Mixed containing 2 of 3, the minimal number is **2** or **3**?\n   417\t\n   418\tI found references to similar puzzles: when the mixed box contains **two types**, and all boxes mislabeled, you need **2 draws**.\n   419\t\n   420\tBut our earlier counterexample suggests 2 is insufficient.\n   421\t\n   422\tWait — but maybe we can choose the **second draw more cleverly**.\n   423\t\n   424\tWhat if, after first draw from “Mixed” → C, we **don’t draw from “Chocolates”**, but from **one of the other pure-labeled bags**, say “Mints”.\n   425\t\n   426\tLet’s try:\n   427\t\n   428\t1. Draw from “Mixed” → C → so true C = “Mixed” bag.\n   429\t2. Draw from “Mints” bag.\n   430\t\n   431\tNow, “Mints” bag ≠ M → so it’s G or Mixed.\n   432\t\n   433\tPossible draws:\n   434\t\n   435\t- If draw **C** → then “Mints” = Mixed (since pure G wouldn’t have C) → Mixed includes C → so Mixed = C+G or C+M\n   436\t- If draw **G** → then could be pure G or Mixed (M+G or C+G)\n   437\t- If draw **M** → impossible? No — if Mixed = C+M, then “Mints” = Mixed → contains M → allowed.\n   438\t\n   439\tSo still ambiguous.\n   440\t\n   441\tBut consider this: **the only bag that can contain a type that matches its label is the Mixed bag**, because pure bags are mislabeled.\n   442\t\n   443\tWait! That’s useful.\n   444\t\n   445\t- Bag labeled “Mints” cannot be pure M, so if you ever draw **M** from it, it **must be Mixed**.\n   446\t- Similarly, draw **G** from “Gum” → must be Mixed.\n   447\t- Draw **C** from “Chocolates” → must be Mixed.\n   448\t\n   449\tAh! This is the key.\n   450\t\n   451\tSo strategy:\n   452\t\n   453\t1. Draw from bag labeled “Mixed” → get X (say C) → so this bag is pure X.\n   454\t2. Now, among the remaining bags, **draw from the bag labeled X** (i.e., “Chocolates”).\n   455\t   - If you draw **X** (C) → then this bag must be Mixed (since it can’t be pure X).\n   456\t   - If you draw **Y ≠ X**, then this bag could be pure Y or Mixed.\n   457\t\n   458\tBut if you draw **Y**, then consider: **can you draw from the bag labeled Y** next?\n   459\t\n   460\t3. Draw from bag labeled Y.\n   461\t\n   462\tNow, if you draw **Y** from bag labeled Y → impossible if pure, so must be Mixed.\n   463\t\n   464\tBut if you draw something else, etc.\n   465\t\n   466\tHowever, in worst case, you might need **3 draws**.\n   467\t\n   468\tBut can we guarantee in **2** by choosing the second draw as **from a bag whose label is not X**?\n   469\t\n   470\tAlternative global insight:\n   471\t\n   472\tThere are only **3 possible configurations** for the Mixed bag: CM, CG, MG.\n   473\t\n   474\tOnce you know the pure C bag (from first draw), the remaining assignment must respect mislabeling.\n   475\t\n   476\tTotal number of valid assignments is small.\n   477\t\n   478\tMaybe **2 draws suffice** if second draw is chosen from a bag that, combined with constraints, eliminates ambiguity.\n   479\t\n   480\tRe-express the earlier ambiguous case:\n   481\t\n   482\t- Observed: “Mixed” bag = C\n   483\t- “Chocolates” bag = M (on draw)\n   484\t\n   485\tAmbiguity: is “Chocolates” pure M or Mixed (C+M)?\n   486\t\n   487\tNow, note: if “Chocolates” were Mixed (C+M), then the pure M bag must be one of the other two: “Mints” or “Gum”.\n   488\t\n   489\tBut “Mints” cannot be M, so pure M must be “Gum”.\n   490\t\n   491\tSimilarly, pure G must be “Mints”.\n   492\t\n   493\tNow, consider the content of the “Mints” bag in each case:\n   494\t\n   495\t- Case 1 (Chocolates = pure M): then “Mints” = pure G or Mixed.\n   496\t   - But Mixed is “Gum” (since only one Mixed), so “Mints” = pure G.\n   497\t- Case 2 (Chocolates = Mixed): then “Mints” = pure G.\n   498\t\n   499\tSo in **both cases**, “Mints” = pure G!\n   500\t\n   501\tWait, is that true?\n   502\t\n   503\tCheck Case 1 again:\n   504\t\n   505\t- Pure C = “Mixed”\n   506\t- Pure M = “Chocolates”\n   507\t- So left: pure G and Mixed\n   508\t- Bags left: “Mints”, “Gum”\n   509\t- “Mints” ≠ M → OK for G or Mixed\n   510\t- “Gum” ≠ G → OK for M (used) or Mixed → so “Gum” must be Mixed\n   511\t- So “Mints” = pure G\n   512\t\n   513\tCase 2:\n   514\t\n   515\t- Pure C = “Mixed”\n   516\t- Mixed = “Chocolates”\n   517\t- So left: pure M and pure G\n   518\t- Bags: “Mints”, “Gum”\n   519\t- “Mints” ≠ M → so must be G\n   520\t- “Gum” ≠ G → so must be M\n   521\t\n   522\tSo again, “Mints” = pure G\n   523\t\n   524\tSo in both ambiguous cases, “Mints” = pure G\n   525\t\n   526\tSimilarly, “Gum” = Mixed in Case 1, pure M in Case 2\n   527\t\n   528\tSo the only difference is “Gum” bag.\n   529\t\n   530\tThus, to resolve, we need to inspect “Gum” bag.\n   531\t\n   532\tDraw one item from “Gum”:\n   533\t\n   534\t- If it’s **M**:\n   535\t   - Could be pure M (Case 2) or Mixed (Case 1, if Mixed = M+G)\n   536\t- If it’s **G**:\n   537\t   - Cannot be pure G (label = Gum), so must be Mixed → Case 1, Mixed = M+G or C+G\n   538\t- If it’s **C**:\n   539\t   - Must be Mixed → Case 1, Mixed = C+G\n   540\t\n   541\tBut if we get **M**, still ambiguous.\n   542\t\n   543\tHowever, note: in Case 1, Mixed = “Gum” = either C+G or M+G.\n   544\t\n   545\tBut can Mixed = C+G in Case 1?\n   546\t\n   547\tIn Case 1, we have:\n   548\t- Pure C = “Mixed”\n   549\t- Pure M = “Chocolates”\n   550\t- Pure G = “Mints”\n   551\t- Mixed = “Gum”\n   552\t\n   553\tMixed must contain two types, but which two? It can't be C+M, because then M would appear in two bags (pure M and Mixed), which is allowed.\n   554\t\n   555\tBut is there any restriction that forces Mixed to include a type whose pure bag is present? No.\n   556\t\n   557\tSo Mixed could be any pair.\n   558\t\n   559\tBut here's the catch: **In Case 1, if Mixed = C+G, then there is no M in Mixed, so total M only in “Chocolates”**.\n   560\t\n   561\tIn Case 2, Mixed = C+M, so M appears in “Chocolates” (Mixed) and “Gum” (pure M).\n   562\t\n   563\tNow, in our observation, we drew M from “Chocolates”.\n   564\t\n   565\t- In Case 1: “Chocolates” = pure M → probability of drawing M = 1\n   566\t- In Case 2: “Chocolates” = Mixed = C+M → probability of drawing M = 0.5\n   567\t\n   568\tBut we’re looking for **guarantee**, not probability.\n   569\t\n   570\tSo still ambiguous.\n   571\t\n   572\tHowever, consider this: **inspect two items from the same bag**.\n   573\t\n   574\tBut the problem says: \"inspect one item at a time (from whichever bag)\" — it doesn’t limit total inspections, just that you inspect sequentially.\n   575\t\n   576\tSo you could inspect **two items from the same bag**.\n   577\t\n   578\tWould that help?\n   579\t\n   580\tIf you inspect two items from “Chocolates” and get **M, M** → still could be pure M or Mixed (just happened to draw two M).\n   581\t\n   582\tBut if you get **M and C** → definitely Mixed.\n   583\t\n   584\tSo in worst case, Mixed bag could fool you with repeated draws of same type.\n   585\t\n   586\tThus, to **guarantee**, you cannot rely on multiple draws from a bag to prove it’s mixed, because you might keep drawing the same type.\n   587\t\n   588\tTherefore, you must use **logical deduction from labels**, not empirical sampling of variety.\n   589\t\n   590\tHence, the only way to guarantee is to **identify the Mixed bag by drawing a type that cannot be in a pure bag given the label**.\n   591\t\n   592\tThus, the optimal strategy:\n   593\t\n   594\t- Draw 1: from “Mixed” → get X → pure X identified.\n   595\t- Draw 2: from bag labeled X → if you get X, then it’s Mixed → done in 2.\n   596\t- If you get Y ≠ X, then this bag is either pure Y or Mixed (X+Y or Y+Z).\n   597\t\n   598\tNow, crucially, **consider the bag labeled Y**.\n   599\t\n   600\t- It cannot be pure Y.\n   601\t- So if you **draw Y from it**, it must be Mixed.\n   602\t\n   603\tBut you haven’t drawn from it yet.\n   604\t\n   605\tSo **third draw**: from bag labeled Y.\n   606\t\n   607\t- If you get Y → then it’s Mixed.\n   608\t- If you get something else, then it’s pure Z, and you can deduce.\n   609\t\n   610\tBut can this always resolve in 3?\n   611\t\n   612\tYes.\n   613\t\n   614\tBecause after three draws, you will have either:\n   615\t- Found a bag that yields a type matching its label → that bag is Mixed.\n   616\t- Or you have enough to deduce by elimination.\n   617\t\n   618\tThus, **3 inspections suffice**.\n   619\t\n   620\tAnd we
